title: NK Cells, the Oxidative Burst, Cytokine Types and Age-Matched Ranges
summary: Learn how NK cells kill without prior sensitisation, which cytokines are type 1 versus type 2, how the NBT and DHR tests detect a failed neutrophil oxidative burst in chronic granulomatous disease, and why children’s lymphocyte subsets need age-matched ranges.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 46 Hits 3, 4 and 5 and Trap 2. NK biology from Hu 2019, Abel 2018, Vojdani 2024 and Wu 2020; cytokine types from Berger 2000 and Zhang & An 2007 (both read via a page-fetch tool) and Lee 2023; NBT, DHR and MPO-deficiency pitfall from Yu 2018 and NADPH oxidase genetics from Arnold 2017; age-related lymphocyte subsets from Zhang 2022, Besci 2021 and Lerkvaleekul 2020. The reviewer presents NBT as the classic CGD screen; Yu 2018 states that DHR flow cytometry has largely superseded it as the gold standard (register flag rv-nbt-superseded-dhr). The reviewer’s “few NK cells” in children (and “reduced/absent at birth” in the Number Vault) holds for NK percentage in one cohort but not for absolute counts in another (rv-pediatric-nk-few-method-dependent). Not taught as fact: the ~10% unstimulated / 80% stimulated NBT reduction figures, that IL-4 specifically suppresses IFN-γ–producing cells (the lesson teaches the source wording that Th2 cells repress Th1 differentiation), and that ranges are hard to establish in the first year of life. Hit 3’s “Type II drive B-cell differentiation” is taught as IL-4 and IL-10 promoting B-cell proliferation and antibody production, with Lee 2023’s qualification that B-cell stimulation is now attributed mainly to Tfh rather than Th2 cells (register flag rv-th2-bcell-help-tfh). The Number Vault table is not taught in full and is not mapped.

objectives: Explain how NK cells recognise and kill targets without prior sensitisation.
Classify IFN-γ, IL-2 and IL-12 as type 1 and IL-4, IL-5, IL-13 and IL-10 as type 2 cytokines.
Interpret NBT and DHR results for chronic granulomatous disease, including the myeloperoxidase-deficiency pitfall.
Explain why lymphocyte subsets in children must be read against age-matched ranges.

scenes.title: Two reports, one baby
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: a 5-month-old with recurrent serious infections. Report 1: nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) slide after PMA stimulation — no blue formazan in the neutrophils. Report 2: lymphocyte panel read against an older-child (7–18 year) range — lymphocytes 6,000/µL flagged high, CD4/CD8 ratio 4.0 flagged high, NK cells 1.2% flagged low. Question token: “Which report is really abnormal?”

cues.text: Invented case: a five-month-old with recurrent serious infections. On the first report, the neutrophils stayed colourless in the NBT test after stimulation.
On the second report, a lymphocyte panel read against an older-child range is flagged three times: high lymphocytes, high CD4 to CD8 ratio, low NK cells.
Which report is really abnormal, and what test would a lab use today?

scenes.title: Killers and messengers
scenes.altText: Left card, NK cells: innate lymphocytes (CD3−CD56+) that kill abnormal or stressed cells without prior sensitisation and without MHC restriction; “missing self” — targets lacking or low in MHC class I lose the inhibitory signal; lytic granules carry perforin, granzymes and granulysin; CD16 (on the CD56dim majority, about 90% of blood NK cells) mediates antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity; CD56bright cells mainly secrete IFN-γ. Right card, cytokine types: Type 1 / Th1 — IFN-γ (main Th1 cytokine, activates macrophages, promotes cell-mediated immunity), IL-2 (from Th1 and NK cells; T- and B-cell proliferation), IL-12 (from macrophages and B cells; drives Th1 and IFN production) — proinflammatory. Type 2 / Th2 — IL-4, IL-5, IL-13 (eosinophils, mast cells, IgE, helminths), IL-10 (anti-inflammatory, promotes B-cell proliferation and antibody production); IL-4 drives Th2 differentiation and Th2 cells repress Th1 differentiation; B-cell stimulation, once credited to Th2 cells, is now thought to be mainly the role of follicular helper T (Tfh) cells.

cues.text: Natural killer cells are innate lymphocytes. They kill abnormal or stressed cells without prior sensitisation and without MHC restriction.

Their cue is missing self: a target with absent or low MHC class one loses the inhibitory brake. They kill with perforin, granzymes and granulysin, and through CD16 they perform antibody-dependent killing.
Type one, or Th1, cytokines drive cellular, proinflammatory immunity: interferon gamma, the main Th1 cytokine; IL-2; and IL-12, made by antigen-presenting cells, which pushes cells toward Th1.

Type two, or Th2, cytokines are IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13, with anti-inflammatory IL-10; IL-4 and IL-10 promote B-cell growth. IL-4 drives Th2 cells, which hold back Th1. Direct B-cell help is now credited mainly to Tfh cells.

props.title: NK cell (CD3− CD56+)
lines: No prior sensitisation, no MHC restriction
Missing self: low MHC I = no brake

scenes.title: When the burst fails
scenes.altText: Mechanism card: in phagocytes the NADPH oxidase (gp91phox and p22phox in the membrane, cytosolic p47phox, p67phox, p40phox) transfers an electron from NADPH to oxygen to form superoxide, the source of hydrogen peroxide and other reactive oxygen species; in chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) the oxidase fails. CYBB (gp91phox) on the X chromosome accounts for about two-thirds of cases. NBT card: neutrophils stimulated with PMA reduce yellow NBT to dark-blue formazan retained in the cell; CGD cells stay unstained; manual readout is semiquantitative and misses many carriers. DHR card: the flow cytometric dihydrorhodamine assay has largely superseded NBT since the late 1990s as the gold standard — easier, more reliable, quantitative, more sensitive, and usually distinguishes X-linked CGD, autosomal recessive CGD and X-linked carriers. Pitfall card: DHR oxidation needs myeloperoxidase (MPO), so complete MPO deficiency can mimic CGD on DHR while NBT is normal; confirm abnormal DHR with gene analysis.

cues.text: Neutrophils kill with an oxidative burst. The NADPH oxidase turns oxygen into superoxide, the source of hydrogen peroxide and other reactive oxygen. In chronic granulomatous disease, the oxidase fails; the X-linked CYBB gene accounts for about two thirds of cases.

In the NBT test, neutrophils are stimulated with PMA in yellow dye. A working oxidase reduces it to dark-blue formazan inside the cell. Cells from a patient with chronic granulomatous disease stay pale. The manual readout is only semiquantitative, and many carriers are missed.

Since the late nineteen-nineties, the flow cytometric dihydrorhodamine assay, DHR, has largely replaced NBT as the gold standard. It is quantitative and more sensitive, and it can usually separate X-linked disease, autosomal recessive disease and X-linked carriers.
One pitfall: DHR needs myeloperoxidase. Complete myeloperoxidase deficiency can look like chronic granulomatous disease on DHR, while NBT stays normal. An abnormal DHR is confirmed by gene analysis.

scenes.title: Read the baby against babies
scenes.altText: Table (Zhang 2022, 813 healthy Chinese children, single-platform flow; medians with 2.5–97.5% intervals): 2–12 months — lymphocytes 4,498/µL (2,309–7,003), CD4/CD8 ratio 2.52 (1.11–5.47), NK 4.12% (1.07–12.23); 7–18 years — lymphocytes 2,043/µL (1,226–4,767), CD4/CD8 1.50 (0.79–3.46), NK 9.96% (1.44–25.51). Neonates 0–1 month: CD4/CD8 3.16, NK 2.51%. In that study’s verification set, intervals used before (from foreign reagent manuals and other studies) fitted worse than the new ones: for example, 80% of 2–12-month CD4/CD8 ratios fell inside the old interval versus 100% inside the new one. Other cohorts: absolute NK counts rose from birth to about 6 months then declined (Besci 2021, cord median 240/mm³, adults 248/mm³); NK percentages differ between regions (Lerkvaleekul 2020). Hook answers: report 2 is normal for a 5-month-old; report 1 suggests a failed oxidative burst — confirm with DHR and gene analysis.

cues.text: In a study of eight hundred and thirteen healthy children, the two-to-twelve-month band had a median of about forty-five hundred lymphocytes per microlitre, with an upper limit near seven thousand; for ages seven to eighteen the median was about two thousand.

The CD4 to CD8 ratio fell with age, from a median of about three in newborns to one and a half in older children. NK percentages rose, from about two and a half percent in newborns to about ten percent. In that study, borrowed older intervals fitted worse: only eighty percent of infant CD4 to CD8 ratios fell inside them.
Other cohorts differ: in one, absolute NK counts rose from birth to six months and then fell, and NK percentages vary between regions. So use age-matched, ideally local, ranges.
Back to the hook. Against an infant range, the lymphocyte panel is normal. The NBT result suggests a failed oxidative burst; confirm with DHR and gene analysis.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “NK cells need prior sensitisation, like T cells” (✓ they kill without prior sensitisation or MHC restriction); “NBT is the modern gold standard for CGD” (✓ DHR flow has largely superseded it; NBT misses many carriers); “Adult or older-child ranges fit a baby” (✓ lymphocyte counts, CD4/CD8 ratio and NK fraction change with age — use age-matched ranges).

cues.text: Trap one: NK cells must be sensitised first, like T cells. No: they kill without prior sensitisation and without MHC restriction.
Trap two: NBT is today’s gold standard for chronic granulomatous disease. No: the DHR flow assay has largely replaced it.
Trap three: an adult range fits a baby. No: lymphocyte counts, the CD4 to CD8 ratio and the NK fraction all change with age.

cues.text: Memory aid: the NK cell is a bouncer with no guest list. No ID badge, meaning no MHC class one, means no entry. The burst is blue ink: working neutrophils turn NBT blue. And a baby needs a baby ruler.

Where it breaks: NK cells also respond to activating stress ligands and can form memory-like cells; DHR, not NBT, is now the main test, and myeloperoxidase deficiency fools it; and infant NK values differ between cohorts and methods.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Three tokens: “NK = innate killing, no prior sensitisation · missing self”, “Type 1 = IFN-γ, IL-2, IL-12 · Type 2 = IL-4, IL-5, IL-13 (+ IL-10)”, “CGD: DHR flow over NBT · children: age-matched ranges”.

cues.text: Natural killer cells kill without prior sensitisation, the dihydrorhodamine flow assay has largely replaced the nitroblue tetrazolium test for chronic granulomatous disease, and a child’s lymphocyte subsets must be read against age-matched ranges.

props.label: NK = innate, no prior sensitisation · missing self
Type 1: IFN-γ, IL-2, IL-12 · Type 2: IL-4, IL-5, IL-13 (+ IL-10)
CGD: DHR over NBT · children: age-matched ranges

explanation.what: Plain language: NK cells are ready-made killers that do not need to have met a threat before; they attack cells that hide their ID badge. Helper T cells send two families of messages: type 1 for cellular, inflammatory defence and type 2 for eosinophil, IgE and antibody-side responses (direct B-cell help is now credited mainly to follicular helper T cells). Neutrophils kill with a chemical burst, and a dye test shows whether that burst works. Children’s blood normally looks different from older people’s, so their results need their own ranges. Scientific terms: natural killer (NK) cell, CD3−CD56+, missing self, MHC class I, perforin, granzymes, granulysin, CD16, antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC), Th1/Th2, IFN-γ, IL-2, IL-12, IL-4, IL-5, IL-10, IL-13, NADPH oxidase, superoxide, chronic granulomatous disease (CGD), nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT), formazan, phorbol myristate acetate (PMA), dihydrorhodamine 123 (DHR), myeloperoxidase (MPO), age-matched reference interval.
explanation.why: NK cells give early innate defence against virus-infected and tumour cells, especially those that lower MHC class I to escape CD8 T cells. The type 1/type 2 split explains which cytokines support killing of intracellular microbes versus eosinophil, IgE and B-cell responses. A failed oxidative burst impairs the killing of ingested bacteria and fungi by phagocytes, which is the defect in CGD. Lymphocyte numbers and proportions change during childhood, so adult or older-child ranges can mislabel a normal infant.
explanation.measure: NK: identified as CD3−CD56+ by flow cytometry. Oxidative burst: NBT slide (yellow dye reduced to blue formazan in stimulated normal neutrophils; semiquantitative) or DHR flow assay (DHR 123 oxidised to fluorescent rhodamine 123; quantitative, usually separates X-linked CGD, autosomal recessive CGD and X-linked carriers); abnormal DHR is confirmed by gene analysis. Paediatric example (Zhang 2022): 2–12 months lymphocytes 4,498/µL (2,309–7,003), CD4/CD8 2.52 (1.11–5.47), NK 4.12%; 7–18 years 2,043/µL, 1.50, 9.96%.
explanation.differs: NK cells (innate, no sensitisation, missing self) vs CD8 cytotoxic T cells (antigen-specific, need MHC class I); type 1 (IFN-γ, IL-2, IL-12; proinflammatory) vs type 2 (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, IL-10; B-cell growth, eosinophils, IgE); NBT (historic, semiquantitative, normal in MPO deficiency) vs DHR (gold standard, quantitative, abnormal in complete MPO deficiency).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: pick the cell that kills without prior sensitisation, sort cytokines into type 1 or type 2, choose the current gold-standard test for CGD or explain an abnormal DHR with normal NBT, and recognise that an infant’s high CD4/CD8 ratio can be normal for age.

questions.stem: A tumour cell has lost MHC class I expression. Which effector cell can still kill it without prior sensitisation?

options.rationale: Correct. NK cells kill without prior sensitisation or MHC restriction, and low MHC class I removes their inhibitory signal (missing self).
Incorrect. CD8 T cells recognise antigen on MHC class I; losing MHC class I is a way tumour cells evade them.
Incorrect. Helper T cells mainly direct immunity through cytokines such as IFN-γ and IL-4; they are not the innate killer here.
Incorrect. B cells receive cytokine help (such as IL-4 and IL-10) to proliferate and make antibody; they are not the innate killer cell.

questions.stem: A patient’s neutrophils show an absent oxidation signal on the dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow assay, but the NBT test is normal and gene sequencing for NADPH oxidase defects is normal. What is the most likely explanation?

options.rationale: Correct. DHR oxidation needs MPO, so MPO deficiency can mimic CGD on DHR while the NBT test and NADPH oxidase genes are normal.
Incorrect. X-linked CGD would also give an abnormal NBT test and a CYBB variant.
Incorrect. A true NADPH oxidase defect would not leave NBT reduction and gene sequencing normal.

options.text: Normal result; DHR cannot detect oxidase defects
options.rationale: Incorrect. DHR is the current gold-standard screen for CGD; the abnormal signal needs an explanation.

questions.stem: Which group lists only type 1 (Th1, cellular) cytokines?

options.rationale: Correct. IFN-γ is the main Th1 cytokine, IL-2 comes from Th1 and NK cells, and IL-12 drives Th1 differentiation and cell-mediated immunity.
Incorrect. These are the classic Th2 cytokines.
Incorrect. IL-4 and IL-10 belong to the type 2 group.
Incorrect. IL-5 and IL-10 belong to the type 2 group.

claims.note: Not taught. No source read gives the 10%/80% NBT figures; Lee 2023 states Th2 cells repress Th1 differentiation rather than the reviewer wording; sources read describe B-cell proliferation and antibody production; NK cells were present at birth in all cohorts read.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 46 Hit 5 presents NBT as the classic CGD screen with ~10% (unstimulated) to 80% (stimulated) reduction. Yu 2018 states that the flow cytometric DHR assay has largely superseded NBT as the gold standard since the late 1990s and that manual NBT often misses carriers; the 10%/80% figures were not found in any source read (register flag rv-nbt-superseded-dhr).

Ch. 46 Trap 2 says children have “few NK cells” (Number Vault: “reduced/absent” at birth). Zhang 2022 found a lower NK percentage in neonates (median 2.51% vs 9.96% at 7–18 years), but Besci 2021 found absolute NK counts in cord blood (median 240/mm³) similar to adults (248/mm³) and higher in infancy, and Lerkvaleekul 2020 reports regional differences. The lesson teaches age-matched ranges without “few NK cells” as a rule (register flag rv-pediatric-nk-few-method-dependent).

Ch. 46 Hit 3 says type II (humoral) cytokines drive B-cell differentiation (Memory Hooks: the “B-helper brew”). Lee 2023 states that B-cell stimulation was once thought to be the role of Th2 cells but is now thought to be the role of follicular helper T (Tfh) cells; Zhang & An 2007 still list IL-4 and IL-10 as promoting B-cell proliferation and IL-10 antibody production. The lesson teaches the cytokine actions with the Tfh qualification (register flag rv-th2-bcell-help-tfh).

morphology.note: No micrographs or NBT slide images; cells and tests are shown as cards.

verification.notes: All taught factual claims checked against open reviews and reference-value studies (Berger 2000 and Zhang & An 2007 read via a page-fetch tool). Several reviewer statements remain pending and untaught. No human expert has reviewed this lesson.
